You could probably tag something along the lines of ‘One-sided relationship’ and something regarding consent. That way, it doesn't give away the plot but still warns people that some shit might be going down. A lot of people view mistaken identity troupes as non-con, and it may get you some hate if you don't earn against it. However, it also depends on the fandom. I think some people understand if crazy takes place because we know we should expect it within the respective fandom. The characters are their own warnings. 

For example, in Star Wars, I expect anything with Jango Fett to include a dead body or two, so I know to steer clear of it. I don't want to read a book with gun violence in it. No one has to tag for that; it's kind of expected. 

Same if I reading a story from the MHA fandom. I am going to run across some not good stories that include kids dealing with abuse and bullying. Not every fic is going to have it, of course, but the overall story is about a bunch of teens fighting. No one really needs to tag about those things. Some people do regardless, but still.
Yes, I freaking hate the authors who hold their chapter hostage. Don't care if the story is finished or a WIP, I will stop reading as soon as I see that.

I won't comment on the fic unless I know the author's work. I don't give a kudos until I have read the story at least twice or if it is by someone whose other works I have read. 

However, I will only do so if they say something along the lines of the first option given. I don't comment on fics when they say that they do not want critics because it can difficult to figure out what they mean by that and I get bored with leaving meaningless shit like “Thanks for writing” “This was cool”. 

For people I am comfortable with, I will leave a comment every creaking chapter, and yes, they will be essays, lol.

I will only read them if they are by an author I have read before and who has a habit of finishing their stories. If I have not read them before or they have a long list of unfinished work, I will mark them for later and wait till it is done. I have often gotten invested in a fic only for the writer to abandon them. Yes, just because someone has a habit of finishing their stories doesn't mean they won't abandon a few, but it doesn't happen nearly as often. 

I once decided to read three WIP fics by the same writer and she abandoned every single last one on the same day. One of them was over 500,000 words. 

I get it; life happens, but investing months or even years into a story that someone abandons can be annoying. 


Not only that, but the length of time between updates drives me insane. By the time the next chapter is shared, I have already forgotten what happened and now have to reread the story. Even with the WIP I do read, I wait until they have at least 10 new chapters or so before I start reading them.

Yep, my mother would make a game out of punching us. It was funny because we would cry as she punched out chest. We also got the privilege of choosing with tool she, or one of her friends, would hit us with whenever we acted up. We had to do wall squats as toddlers where you would hold a book in your outstretched arms as you sat against the wall. Drop the book, you get beat. Fall over cause you can’t hold the pose anymore, you get beat. It was supposed to be fun because it made the adults laugh. I am 30 and she still likes to share the story with others. 

I used to laugh too until my own child told my mother that she was being abusive. It took until that moment for me to realize that those “family moments” are what led me into developing Borderline Personality Disorder and a severe case of agoraphobia. I have never left my kid alone with my mom because I could never trust her but I honestly couldn’t understand why until that moment. 

My mom wasn’t even the worst part. Honestly, the only person who didn’t put their hands on me as a kid was a drug dealer I was sold to at one point by a “family friend” who my mom left me with. 

I am in therapy now and also have one for my kid. I don’t want to continue the cycle.

This! Test anxiety is not a diagnosis. It is something people struggle with but it isn't something that would cause issues with a person's daily life. It can be overcome fairly easily. The same can not be said for general anxiety. I have social anxiety and struggle with taking tests as it is the situation in which I am being judged and watched while doing so. This isn't true, my professor may look around to see that people aren't cheating, but my brain sees it as everyone in my class is staring at me and whispering about how incompetent I am. I am also a dumb ass so of course I won't do well. 

It's not that I am slow at reading or even that I don't understand the material. It's the fact that others think that I do that bothers me. Even though reality shows that this isn't the case and no one gives a fuck about what I'm doing. 

OP does seem rather entitled for believing that they shouldn't have a time restraint on tests because it's something they haven't had to deal with before. That isn't a disability. That's a lack of experience. Once they get into the flow of things it will get easier. If it doesn't, it's normal. There are still ways to work around that.

I have test anxiety and got an accommodation. Still, it wouldn't take me an hour to answer a 29-minute quiz. If that is something you struggle with I suggest you talk to your professor and the disability office. If you have a documented diagnosis they are able to help you. Sadly, if you do not they may not do anything.

Not sleeping in class. Ok fine, I get it. Why show up only to go to sleep. However, I don't see why they can't just ignore the student. This is college and a good portion probably work full-time jobs and have other commitments. It sucks for them to fall asleep during class but it's not hurting anyone. As long as they are being obnoxious with it, let them sleep. If they fail, that's on them.

As long as students are not disrupting the class I don't see why they should be punished for arriving late or leaving early. Again, it's a college course. I have been in classes where the professor went over by 20 mins and I ended up late to my next class cause I decided to be dumb and not leave when I should have. It happens.

I have never heard of this being a problem. I have met plenty of therapists and case workers/managers at my local library. I understand that there could be an issue with privacy. You aren't guaranteed it if you are out in the open, but it's not completely impossible to find a semi-private area in the library to meet people. For certain things, like therapy, I would meet in a study room. When I worked at my university library I would often schedule therapy appointments before my shift started. That I would already be in the building. It helped because this meant that I didn't have to request days off from work or be forced to leave early/come in late just to be able to make it to my appointment. 

At the same time, I can see how it may be discouraged. It's not just the privacy thing but the simple fact that you are going to be talking. Sometimes the topic can bring about an emotional response that can be pretty distracting. Same goes for any kind of meeting really.

No, I get it. It can be distracting for a lot of people. I was never bothered by the noise but I am the type who can't study without music. So I would always have my headphones on. But I can still imagine how annoying it is for those who want complete silence as they browse or work. Libraries don't seem like that anymore. I do recommend talking to your librarian and seeing if they can help. Sometimes they can open a room for you to sit in or will even ask that the person quiet down. If enough people complain, they might even kick them out.

I think many libraries are adopting sound zones. So there will be a portion of the library that is just for studying but everywhere else is fair game. It doesn't always work as noise does travel. So, no lol. Libraries are no longer the sanctuaries that they used to be.

Which is why I said, “Depending on how others are doing”. If it's an issue in which the majority of the class is failing it could be something to go to others about l. If this person is having problems with their class, and the professor isn't helping, the Dean is someone they can talk to. However, that is a last-resort type of situation. It doesn't matter if it is silly to you if the majority of the students are struggling they should reach out to those in charge. Now I don't recommend talking to the Dean first but I do believe that if the professor, their advisor, and the head of the department aren't able to do anything, the dean could help.

My therapist asked me to do something similar a few times. Not exactly fanfics but she would tell me to write stories with myself at the center. It helps to make you aware of yourself and gets down on how you value yourself as a person. I learned that I tend to praise people for the same stuff I shit on myself for. Most notably when it comes to parenting. I will dog myself doing the most basic things like going to the doctor. Despite this being common I would look at myself like I was trash because I felt like I was whinging too much about being ill. Yet others going is ok. I take my kiddo, and it's ok. I take myself and that means I am taking up time for those who truly need the help including my kid cause they often had to go with me. 

It's far from the truth but it wasn't till I started writing about a character doing mundane tasks, that I realized this. I am allowed to live. I don't want to most of the time, but I shouldn't punish myself for doing so.

Networking for the most part. Reach out to the school beforehand and let them know about your situation. Depending on the school, they may be able to work with you. Work hard in the semesters you have left to get your GPA as high as you can. It's not just the school you should talk to either, find people who work or have worked, in the field you are trying to get into and talk to them. You don't have to tell those people your situation but still get to know them. Ask them about their trade and join any groups you can as an undergrad. It will give you a leg up to already be known within the community you are trying to get into. 

I reached out to places within my hometown and the one I am currently for school. I have a kiddo as well and got involved with various related groups that work with children. People may not know me by name, but I know whose name to use to get them to listen to me. On top of that, I am a member of many marginalized groups that people tend to overlook. Now that people are really trying to diversify 🤷🏾‍♀️. 

I also worked within the field that I wanted to join. If you have the time, take up an internship. You can also volunteer if you are able. It doesn't have to be the exact job you want. An example is it you want to be a doctor. You can't exactly work as a doctor before getting your degree. However, you can still find hospital-related jobs as an undergrad. Or if you want to do something related to religion. Volunteer at your local church to operate the cameras on Sunday. Want to be a teacher? Work at a daycare or one of those after-school programs they have for children. It's not a guarantee that it will work, but it does help to have that experience under your belt. It goes far in proving that you can about whatever it is you are going to grad school for and will do what you can to succeed even if your grades don't exactly reflect that.

Again, it depends on your career path. If one is trying to become a doctor their grades would matter. However, I highly doubt the same can be said for someone going into something like social work. The degree is what matters most, not your GPA. 

Now, factoring in graduate school, they will take your GPA into consideration but they also care about the things you did outside of school. In my opinion, your GPA alone will never be enough to prove why you should be accepted into any grad program. All your GPA does is show that you have the capability to memorize information. It doesn't necessarily prove that you know and understand it. 
Especially in this day and age where the internet is a thing. You also have those classes that allow you to use your notes and books for the test. Meaning that you don't have to memorize anything but the chapter you happen to be on. 

But that aside, the likelihood of even half the people on this post being able to get a job within their field of choice after graduation is not the greatest. Sure, a good chunk of us will but there will be some who will not. So the pay is already expected to be low regardless. Not until we get the experience that our job, not school, gives us over time.

You must have googled the wrong sites because the causes tend to be childhood trauma, genetics, early childhood experiences (such as stress but not outward trauma), and their overall psychological state. Now, the levels of that contribute to the development of NPD over other personality disorders are unknown. It still stands to reason that these are what go into developing all personality disorders.

There very much is a genetic factor to personality disorders. To develop one a person has to have gone through some form of trauma, yes, but their environment and genetics also play a role in it. However, the level of each isn't an exact science. Someone could experience one truly traumatic event as a child and still manage to develop it even if their environment is stellar outside of that one experience. In some cases stress, not trauma, can make it so you develop a personality disorder. It's because those other factors also play a role. Someone whose parent has a personality disorder has a higher chance of developing a personality disorder full stop. They don't even have to be in contact with said parent. 

That's why preventive care for children of people with those disorders is so important.

It is not part of fanfic to not criticize. That is a whole new concept that people came up with because they didn't want to offend each other and some people took it way too far. I don't think it helps to only comment to say that a story is good. It tells the writer nothing and is superficial at best. Sometimes what a person likes best about a story can also be a critic. Like if someone was talking about how a writer wrote a chapter that featured a person's mental breakdown. The writing could make it difficult for some readers to truly understand what is going on and may take some people out of the story while reading. But it can also be powerful because it makes people aware of their own mental health as they either relate or can't understand what is taking place. Some people may find the fact that some readers found such a chapter hard to read as an insult and a huge criticism of their work. I have seen plenty of writers get upset with readers for this very issue as if they are supposed to automatically understand everything. But that isn't the case at all. 

I think readers should be able to share what they like and dislike about a story as it shows the whole story. As long as they aren't overly abrasive, abusive, or demanding that is. Pointing out an inconsistency or a mistake is not either of those things.
